objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Read probability notation
teach.text: An outcome is one result. The sample space S lists all possible results; an event A is a set of results. P(A) is between 0 and 1. A probability of 0.25 means 25%, not 25 successes guaranteed in every 100 trials.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Read probability notation
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: For one fair die, S={1,2,3,4,5,6}. Event A={2,4,6} means an even result.
steps: Identify the three outcomes in A.

practice.prompt: What is the sample space for one toss of a coin?
practice.rationale: The sample space includes every possible outcome.

practice.prompt: A probability is 0.35. What percentage is equivalent?
practice.rationale: Multiply a probability by 100 to express it as a percentage.

practice.prompt: Which value cannot be a probability?
practice.rationale: Probabilities cannot exceed 1 or fall below 0.

vocab: One result of a chance process.
The set of all possible outcomes.
A set of outcomes from the sample space.
A measure of likelihood from 0 to 1.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Use equally likely outcomes
teach.text: For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=favorable outcomes / total outcomes. Count the same kind of outcome in numerator and denominator. This counting rule needs equally likely outcomes; a biased spinner needs its actual sector probabilities.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Use equally likely outcomes
anchorChart.rule: For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=favorable outcomes / total outcomes.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A fair eight-sector spinner has three red sectors.

practice.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. What is P(result greater than 4)?
practice.rationale: The favorable outcomes are 5 and 6: 2/6=1/3.

practice.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 6 green tokens. One token is selected uniformly. What is P(red)?
practice.rationale: The total is 10, so 4 favorable tokens give 4/10.

practice.prompt: When does favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes apply directly?
practice.rationale: Counting outcomes directly assumes equal probabilities.

vocab: A probability calculated from an assumed model rather than observed counts.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Estimate from observations
teach.text: Empirical probability is observed successes / trials. With many independent repetitions under the same conditions, relative frequency tends toward the underlying probability. More trials do not force an exact match or make a losing streak require a win next.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Estimate from observations
anchorChart.rule: Empirical probability is observed successes / trials.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A machine produces 14 defective parts among 200 inspected parts.
steps: Use all 200 inspections as the denominator.

practice.prompt: A player succeeds in 18 of 60 attempts. What is the empirical probability of success?
A fair coin has just landed tails five times. What is P(heads on the next independent toss)?
practice.rationale: Earlier independent tosses do not change the next probability.

practice.prompt: What does the law of large numbers suggest?
options: Each short run must balance exactly
Relative frequency tends toward the underlying probability as trials accumulate
The next result corrects the last result
A large number of trials makes events independent
practice.rationale: It concerns long-run proportions, not compensation on the next trial.

vocab: Observed event occurrences divided by the number of trials.
Under suitable repeated-trial conditions, observed proportions tend toward the underlying probability.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Separate independent from dependent
teach.text: Independent events do not change each other’s probability: P(B|A)=P(B). For independent events, P(A and B)=P(A)P(B). Drawing without replacement usually changes the next draw’s probability because the bag’s contents change.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Separate independent from dependent
anchorChart.rule: Independent events do not change each other’s probability: P(B|A)=P(B).
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw two without replacement.
steps: After red is removed, 2 red remain among 4 tokens.

practice.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled independently. What is P(two sixes)?
practice.rationale: Multiply 1/6 by 1/6.

practice.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. After a red token is removed, what is P(red on the next draw)?
practice.rationale: There are now 2 red tokens among 4 total tokens.

practice.prompt: Which statement defines independence?
options: Knowing one event occurred does not change the probability of the other
practice.rationale: Independence is about unchanged conditional probability.

vocab: Events for which learning that one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
Events whose probabilities change when another event is known to occur.
The probability of an event within the group specified by a condition.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Disjoint does not mean independent
teach.text: Disjoint, or mutually exclusive, events cannot occur together: P(A and B)=0. If both have positive probability, they are not independent: learning that one occurred rules out the other.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Disjoint does not mean independent
anchorChart.rule: Disjoint, or mutually exclusive, events cannot occur together: P(A and B)=0.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: For one die roll, A={1,3,5} and B={2,4,6}.
steps: No outcome is in both sets.
If A happened, B is impossible on that roll.

practice.prompt: On one die roll, are getting a 1 and getting a 6 disjoint?
options: Yes, one roll cannot have both results
No, both are possible in the sample space
Only if the die is biased
practice.rationale: A single outcome cannot simultaneously be 1 and 6.

practice.prompt: Two disjoint events each have positive probability. Are they independent?
options: Yes if their probabilities are equal
practice.rationale: Occurrence of one changes the probability of the other to zero.

practice.prompt: A and B are disjoint with P(A)=0.2 and P(B)=0.3. What is P(A and B)?
practice.rationale: Disjoint events have no overlap.

vocab: Events that cannot happen together; also called mutually exclusive.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Read all four Venn regions
teach.text: A Venn diagram separates A only, both, B only, and neither. The rectangle represents the full sample space. Include the overlap when counting all of A or all of B; count it once for the union.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Read all four Venn regions
anchorChart.rule: A Venn diagram separates A only, both, B only, and neither.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: Among 40 students, 18 take math, 12 take science, and 5 take both.

practice.prompt: 18 students take math and 5 of them also take science. How many take math only?
practice.rationale: Remove the overlap: 18−5=13.

practice.prompt: A Venn diagram has A-only=9, both=4, B-only=7, neither=10. How many are in A?
practice.rationale: All of A includes A-only and the overlap: 9+4=13.

practice.prompt: In that same diagram, how many are outside both circles?
practice.rationale: Neither is the region outside both circles.

visuals.title: 40 students: 13 math only, 5 both, 7 science only, 15 neither
visuals.alt: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: math only 13, both 5, science only 7, neither 15. Total 40.

d772-s3-l3-1.visualLabel: ILLUSTRATIVE VENN DIAGRAM • ORIGINAL PRACTICE DATA
vocab: A diagram showing event membership and overlap within a sample space.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: OR is the inclusive union
teach.text: A union B, written A ∪ B, includes A, B, or both. P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Subtract the overlap once because adding both probabilities counts it twice.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: OR is the inclusive union
anchorChart.rule: A union B, written A ∪ B, includes A, B, or both.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

practice.prompt: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.3, and P(both)=0.1. What is P(A or B)?
In probability, inclusive OR means:
options: A or B, but never both
practice.rationale: Union includes outcomes in either event, including the overlap.

practice.prompt: Disjoint events have probabilities 0.25 and 0.35. What is the probability of either?
practice.rationale: No overlap is subtracted, so 0.25+0.35=0.60.

visuals.title: 40 students: 13 math only, 5 both, 7 science only, 15 neither
visuals.alt: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: math only 13, both 5, science only 7, neither 15. Total 40.

d772-s3-l3-2.visualLabel: ILLUSTRATIVE VENN DIAGRAM • ORIGINAL PRACTICE DATA
vocab: Outcomes in A, B, or both; the inclusive OR event.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: AND is the intersection
teach.text: A intersection B, written A ∩ B, contains the overlap. In general P(A and B)=P(A)P(B|A). Use P(A)P(B) only when independence is justified; without replacement usually requires the changed second probability.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: AND is the intersection
anchorChart.rule: A intersection B, written A ∩ B, contains the overlap.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: Of 40 students, 5 take both math and science.

practice.prompt: A fair coin and a fair die are independent. What is P(heads and a 6)?
practice.rationale: Multiply 1/2 by 1/6.

practice.prompt: A bag has 2 gold and 3 silver tokens. Draw two without replacement. What is P(two gold)?
Which Venn region represents A ∩ B?
options: Both circles including their outer regions
practice.rationale: Intersection means membership in both events.

visuals.title: 40 students: 13 math only, 5 both, 7 science only, 15 neither
visuals.alt: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: math only 13, both 5, science only 7, neither 15. Total 40.

d772-s3-l3-3.visualLabel: ILLUSTRATIVE VENN DIAGRAM • ORIGINAL PRACTICE DATA
vocab: Outcomes belonging to both events; the AND event.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: NOT is the complement
teach.text: The complement Aᶜ contains every outcome not in A. P(not A)=1−P(A). For at least one success, the complementary event is no successes. Multiply failure probabilities only if the trials are independent.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: NOT is the complement
anchorChart.rule: The complement Aᶜ contains every outcome not in A.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A shipment arrives on time with probability 0.82.
steps: On time and not on time cover all outcomes.

practice.prompt: P(A)=0.72. What is P(not A)?
Two independent trials each succeed with probability 0.2. What is P(at least one success)?
practice.rationale: P(no successes)=0.8×0.8=0.64; complement is 0.36.

practice.prompt: What is the complement of at least one head in three coin tosses?
practice.rationale: The only way to fail to get at least one head is to get no heads.

visuals.title: 40 students: 13 math only, 5 both, 7 science only, 15 neither
visuals.alt: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: math only 13, both 5, science only 7, neither 15. Total 40.

d772-s3-l3-4.visualLabel: ILLUSTRATIVE VENN DIAGRAM • ORIGINAL PRACTICE DATA
vocab: All outcomes in the sample space that are not in the event.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Calculate a probability-weighted mean
teach.text: Expected value is E(X)=Σ xP(x): multiply each outcome value by its probability, then add. A valid discrete distribution has nonnegative probabilities totaling 1. Do not use an unweighted average unless all outcomes are equally likely.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Calculate a probability-weighted mean
anchorChart.rule: Expected value is E(X)=Σ xP(x): multiply each outcome value by its probability, then add.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A game pays $20 with probability 0.10 and $0 otherwise. A ticket costs $3.
steps: Use net values: $17 when winning and −$3 otherwise.

practice.prompt: X is 0 with probability 0.75 and 8 with probability 0.25. What is E(X)?
Which is a valid probability distribution?
practice.rationale: Both probabilities are nonnegative and total 1.

practice.prompt: A ticket costs $2 and pays $10 with probability 0.2, otherwise $0. What is the expected NET value?
practice.rationale: Expected payout is $2; subtract the $2 cost to get $0.

vocab: A probability-weighted average of numerical outcomes.
Possible discrete values with nonnegative probabilities that total 1.

objectives: Explain the denominator, relationship, or net value before calculating.

teach.title: Interpret long-run value and risk
teach.text: Expected value is a long-run average, not a promised result on the next trial; it may not be a possible single outcome. For a decision, compare net values consistently and consider variability, affordability, and model assumptions.

memory: Read the event and conditions before choosing a rule.

anchorChart.title: Interpret long-run value and risk
anchorChart.rule: Expected value is a long-run average, not a promised result on the next trial; it may not be a possible single outcome.
columns: Define the sample space or conditioning group.
Justify the rule; do not multiply or add automatically.

weDo.prompt: A service charges $18. It pays a $250 repair bill with probability 0.04.
steps: Expected provider margin before other expenses=$18−$10=$8.
That average does not guarantee an $8 margin on one customer.

practice.prompt: A game has expected net value −$0.50. What does this mean?
options: The long-run average loss is $0.50 per play
A win becomes due after losses
practice.rationale: Individual plays vary; the expectation describes the average over repetitions.

practice.prompt: One fair die has expected value 3.5. Is 3.5 possible on a single roll?
options: No; an expected value need not be an individual outcome
Only after an odd number of rolls
The expected value must be wrong
practice.rationale: The mean can fall between possible outcomes.

practice.prompt: Plan A has expected net value $4; Plan B has $2. Which statement is supported?
options: A guarantees more money on the next trial
A has a higher long-run average under the stated models
practice.rationale: A higher expectation alone does not determine one-trial results or variability.

vocab: Payout or benefit after subtracting the cost.
How much individual outcomes differ; expectation alone does not describe this risk.

teach.title: Read all four Venn regions
teach.text: A Venn diagram separates A only, both, B only, and neither. The rectangle represents the full sample space. Include the overlap when counting all of A or all of B; count it once for the union.

teach.title: OR is the inclusive union
teach.text: A union B, written A ∪ B, includes A, B, or both. P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Subtract the overlap once because adding both probabilities counts it twice.

teach.title: AND is the intersection
teach.text: A intersection B, written A ∩ B, contains the overlap. In general P(A and B)=P(A)P(B|A). Use P(A)P(B) only when independence is justified; without replacement usually requires the changed second probability.

teach.title: NOT is the complement
teach.text: The complement Aᶜ contains every outcome not in A. P(not A)=1−P(A). For at least one success, the complementary event is no successes. Multiply failure probabilities only if the trials are independent.

d772-s3-review.overview: Combine probability types, event relationships, set operations, and expected value.
objectives: Explain expected value as a long-run net average.

teach.title: Read probability notation
teach.text: An outcome is one result. The sample space S lists all possible results; an event A is a set of results. P(A) is between 0 and 1. A probability of 0.25 means 25%, not 25 successes guaranteed in every 100 trials.

teach.title: Use equally likely outcomes
teach.text: For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=favorable outcomes / total outcomes. Count the same kind of outcome in numerator and denominator. This counting rule needs equally likely outcomes; a biased spinner needs its actual sector probabilities.

teach.title: Estimate from observations
teach.text: Empirical probability is observed successes / trials. With many independent repetitions under the same conditions, relative frequency tends toward the underlying probability. More trials do not force an exact match or make a losing streak require a win next.

teach.title: Separate independent from dependent
teach.text: Independent events do not change each other’s probability: P(B|A)=P(B). For independent events, P(A and B)=P(A)P(B). Drawing without replacement usually changes the next draw’s probability because the bag’s contents change.

teach.title: Disjoint does not mean independent
teach.text: Disjoint, or mutually exclusive, events cannot occur together: P(A and B)=0. If both have positive probability, they are not independent: learning that one occurred rules out the other.
